This occurs within a bounded domain, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, where the Navier-Strokes equations are driven by a source term derived from the elliptic equation.

This study examines the application of the Big Five personality framework to assess individuals' susceptibility to drug use and misuse. It introduces a novel dataset comprising Big Five scores for 1,000 participants, derived from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP), alongside self-reported histories of drug consumption. Utilizing this dataset, the research evaluates the efficacy of various classification models in predicting drug-related behaviors. Furthermore, it investigates the influence of data preprocessing techniques, specifically the use of imputation strategies and normalization, on model performance.

Humans possess an extensive capacity for commonsense reasoning, a trait that has long been a focal point of research in artificial intelligence. However, the vast majority of existing commonsense knowledge repositories prioritize semantic associations over inferential capabilities. To address this gap, we introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive knowledge base dedicated to capturing explicit atomic-level abduction and deduction rules. We further present a novel semantic similarity metric specifically designed to evaluate the relevance of abduction and deduction rules within ATOMIC. This metric facilitates the retrieval of pertinent rules for abduction, thereby enhancing the performance of commonsense reasoning tasks.

This study examines the application of the HHL quantum algorithm for portfolio optimization, with a specific focus on the classical-quantum interface. We propose a hybrid framework where classical components handle preprocessing and postprocessing, while quantum components execute the HHL algorithm. Our analysis highlights that the HHL implementation must satisfy three critical conditions: (1) the Hamiltonian matrix must be efficiently diagonalizable, (2) the condition number must be effectively estimated, and (3) the initial state must be prepared with high fidelity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quantum circuit can be decomposed into modular components, allowing for execution across multiple interconnected quantum devices.

This study introduces a novel multimodal training framework designed to enhance data efficiency in end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) models. Achieving superior performance in this domain requires addressing two key challenges: (1) effectively integrating complementary information from both audio and text modalities, and (2) leveraging the vast volume of available textual data to improve performance on scarce audio samples. To address these issues, we propose a two-stage approach. Initially, we introduce a Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning (CMCL) module that learns cross-modal representations by contrasting audio against text. Subsequently, we introduce a Text-Enhanced Cross-Modal Attention (TECMA) module that refines audio features using text information. Furthermore, to maximize the utility of extensive text-only datasets, we develop a Text-Only Pretraining (TOP) module that trains a text encoder to generate robust text-enhanced audio representations. Experimental results on the VoxLip-Kits dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines the average cross-sectional area of shapes in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, defined by the integral of the $d$-dimensional volume of planar slices passing through the shape. We derive a general formula for this average cross section applicable to any shape with a specified $d$-dimensional volume and surface area. Applying this result, we demonstrate that the average cross section is maximized when the shape is a sphere, provided the volume and surface area remain constant. Furthermore, we derive an asymptotic expression for the average cross section when the shape is a large sphere containing a small inclusion, showing that the leading-order term depends solely on the volume and surface area of the inclusion.

This study examines the random uniform parking function $f_n$ of length $n$, defined as the composition of $n$ independent and identically distributed uniform random variables on $\{1, \dots, n\}$. We analyze the initial $k_n$ entries of $f_n$, where $k_n$ grows proportionally to $n$ as $n \to \infty$. Our findings demonstrate that, in the limit, these initial entries converge to a specific non-trivial distribution. Furthermore, we establish that the joint distribution of these initial entries admits a representation as a determinantal point process characterized by a kernel derived from the solution to a Riemann-Hilbert problem.

We report on the observation of a DC conduction blockade in superconducting nanowires, which occurs when the wire is threaded by a magnetic flux slightly exceeding one flux quantum. This phenomenon is attributed to the formation of a single, long Josephson junction along the nanowire's length. This finding offers a novel method for fabricating Josephson junctions with tunable critical currents and presents a promising avenue for developing superconducting nanowire-based quantum bits.

The brown dwarf GJ 229B has been extensively studied for over three decades, serving as a benchmark for atmospheric research. While its fundamental parameters, such as effective temperature and surface gravity, have been derived from spectroscopic data, these estimates have historically varied significantly. This study presents a Bayesian atmospheric retrieval analysis of the near-infrared spectra (1.1–2.5 µm) obtained from the Keck/NIRSPEC and Gemini/NIRI instruments. The analysis incorporates a comprehensive forward model featuring a 1D radiative-convective structure, a 1D chemistry module, and a 1D cloud/haze scheme. By utilizing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework to explore a 12-parameter model space—including molecular abundances, cloud properties, and atmospheric circulation—we find that the data are most consistent with a clear atmosphere devoid of clouds. The results indicate an effective temperature of 900 ± 100 K and a mass of 28.5 ± 1.5 M_Jup, which aligns with the theoretical evolutionary track of the object. Furthermore, the study reveals a strong positive correlation between the retrieved mass and the atmospheric mean meridional circulation strength.

We examine the implications of a thermal environment on the Bjorken scaling behavior of structure functions. We demonstrate that, within the leading logarithmic approximation, the parton distribution function (PDF) for a thermal medium can be derived by convolving a vacuum PDF with a thermal weight function. This derivation relies on the assumption that the PDF remains invariant under a longitudinal boost. We further show that this invariance is satisfied when the thermal medium consists of a thermalized vacuum PDF combined with thermalized partons. Under these specific conditions, we derive the Bjorken scaling structure functions and determine the corresponding PDF.

We introduce a new method for generating novel view videos that can be predicted from a single image, supporting an angular range of up to 40° from the original image. Our approach employs a dual-branch architecture designed to jointly optimize both the novel view synthesis and the motion estimation tasks. Specifically, the motion branch utilizes a recurrent module to estimate motion vectors from a sequence of images, while the view generation branch leverages these motion vectors to create the novel view from the source image. By integrating these components, our model achieves superior performance in both motion estimation and novel view generation compared to existing methods.

Inter-orbital coupling, a phenomenon recently recognized as vital for the advancement of quantum information and spintronics, has long been elusive in photonic systems. This study demonstrates that such coupling can be achieved in a photonic lattice by utilizing a single, linearly polarized light beam to excite multiple orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes. The mechanism relies on the interplay between the lattice's spatial symmetry and the symmetry of OAM states, which together facilitate the transfer of OAM within the lattice. This approach enables the creation of a robust, all-photonic system capable of supporting multi-level quantum bits (qubits) and qutrits. Furthermore, the study reveals that the resulting inter-orbital coupling is highly tunable through the manipulation of lattice parameters.

We examine the $1^-$ negative-parity excited states of the $\Omega^-$ baryon, which carries two units of strangeness and consists of three $s$ quarks. Our analysis utilizes the Godfrey-Isgur (GI) model, incorporating a color-Coulomb interaction alongside a confinement potential defined by a linear term and a quadratic term. We determine the masses of these excited $\Omega^-$ states by fitting the model parameters to experimental data on $\Lambda$ and $\Sigma$ baryons. Our results indicate that the $1^-$ excited $\Omega^-$ mass is predicted to be $2.20$ GeV, with a mass splitting of $0.11$ GeV relative to the ground state $\Omega^-$ baryon.

This study employs a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) approach to simulate airflow and the dispersion of virus-carrying aerosols within an enclosed room. The research specifically examines the impact of various parameters, including airflow velocity, airflow direction, and the quantity of virus-carrying aerosols. The findings indicate that airflow velocity and direction are the primary determinants of the airflow field and the spatial distribution of these aerosols. Furthermore, the study highlights that the concentration of virus-carrying aerosols increases proportionally with the amount of aerosols released.

We introduce a novel scattering mechanism termed birefringent scattering, wherein x-rays are deflected by the intense electromagnetic field of a laser. This effect arises from the modification of the refractive index within the laser field, which induces a Faraday rotation of the x-ray polarization. We demonstrate that this phenomenon enables the generation of a focused, circularly polarized x-ray beam through the scattering of linearly polarized x-rays off a linearly polarized laser.

This note introduces the concept of fully transitive polyhedra and demonstrates that there are exactly 28 such structures, which encompass all known transitive polyhedra. Additionally, we present an algorithm designed to generate these forms.

We introduce the concept of unclonable encryption, a framework designed to prevent adversaries from generating multiple ciphertexts that decrypt to the same message. Our approach demonstrates the existence of an adaptively secure unclonable encryption scheme within the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM). Furthermore, we establish a connection between unclonable encryption and quantum extractable witness indistinguishability, utilizing this relationship to derive an unclonable encryption scheme from any quantum extractable witness-indistinguishable proof system.

This paper examines information-theoretic authentication within a physical layer framework where an adversary has access to the channel. We demonstrate that, in the presence of an adversary who can compromise a fraction $p$ of the transmitted bits, the physical layer can achieve information-theoretic authentication if and only if $p < 1/2$. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, information-theoretically secure authentication scheme that operates under the condition $p < 1/2$.

Twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are predicted to host low-damped and quasi-flat plasmon modes, which are characterized by their minimal dispersion. We demonstrate that these modes can be observed in twisted bilayer $WSe_2$ through scanning gate microscopy. The experimental findings align with theoretical calculations, revealing that these modes emerge when plasmon resonances from individual layers couple to form a collective state. This phenomenon occurs specifically under conditions of strong interlayer coupling and weak dielectric screening.

This study examines the properties of gradient almost conformal Ricci solitons on Sasakian manifolds. We demonstrate that the associated potential function remains constant for any almost conformal gradient soliton on an Einstein Sasakian manifold. Furthermore, we derive an explicit characterization for the potential function of an almost conformal gradient soliton on a Sasakian $\eta$-Einstein manifold. Finally, we establish the non-existence of almost conformal gradient solitons on Sasakian space forms with non-zero curvature.

Massive stars, which are crucial for the chemical evolution of the cosmos, exhibit mass loss rates that are significantly higher than those of lower-mass stars such as our Sun. While the general mechanism behind this phenomenon is understood to be radiative line-driven winds, the specific details of how these lines interact with radiation remain poorly constrained. To address this, we have developed a new, highly parallelized radiative transfer code that utilizes a discrete ordinate method to solve the radiative transfer equations. This code is designed to handle complex, three-dimensional geometries and incorporates a novel approach for modeling the interaction between radiation and spectral lines. We applied this tool to simulate the wind of a 15 solar mass star, comparing our results against the well-established CMFGEN code. Our simulations indicate that the new code accurately reproduces the observable characteristics of the stellar wind, including the spectral line profiles and the emergent spectrum. Furthermore, the code is sufficiently efficient to facilitate extensive three-dimensional modeling of radiatively driven winds.

Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) is known to increase at a surface or interface when adjacent to a material with strong SOC, a phenomenon termed interface-enhanced SOC. This study investigates the origin of this effect within the Rashba model, demonstrating that SOC is amplified at interfaces due to the confinement of electrons to a narrow region. This confinement results in a substantial rise in the effective electric field perpendicular to the interface, which in turn significantly boosts the SOC strength.

This study presents bound state solutions for a fractional Schrödinger equation with a general potential form $V(x) = m^{\alpha} [g_1 |x|^{\sigma} + g_2 |x|^{-\sigma}]$, where $g_1, g_2, m, \sigma,$ and $\alpha$ are arbitrary parameters. The solution is derived using the path integral formalism, with the fractional kinetic energy defined via the Riesz fractional derivative. The resulting wave functions are expressed in terms of Whittaker functions, and the corresponding energy spectrum is provided analytically.

We introduce a novel approach to training neural networks that incorporates Lipschitz constraints, specifically targeting the reduction of overfitting in models with excessive capacity. Our method employs a new, differentiable approximation of the Lipschitz constant, which is grounded in the spectral norm of the Jacobian matrix. This approximation is derived from a sum of squared singular values, a formulation that facilitates efficient computation via backpropagation. We validate our approach through experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, demonstrating that our technique achieves superior generalization performance compared to existing methods that impose similar constraints.

This study introduces a Basque agreement dataset designed to evaluate neural networks' ability to predict grammatical agreement. We compare English and Basque agreement tasks using sequential and recurrent models, finding that while English achieves high accuracy, Basque agreement prediction lags significantly behind. We attribute this disparity to the necessity of incorporating morphological information, a factor we address by integrating it into the model architecture.

We investigate the orbital dynamics and radiative characteristics of exoplanets in highly eccentric trajectories. We introduce a novel analytical framework for computing the time-averaged insolation across various orbital periods and durations of stellar exposure. Furthermore, we examine the orbital evolution of exoplanets subject to significant eccentricity variations, utilizing a Hamiltonian formulation to derive the secular evolution of the system's eccentricity and argument of periastron.

Repetitive exercises are essential for rehabilitation, yet they often lack motivation. This study investigates whether modified digital games can enhance motivation for repetitive tasks, specifically focusing on a change to the "Pac-Man" game to support the treatment of motor disorders. The proposed adaptation introduces a new control scheme where the player's avatar moves in response to the user's gaze direction, eliminating the need for manual input. This modification allows for hands-free operation, making the game particularly suitable for individuals with motor impairments. Additionally, the study introduces a scoring system that rewards the player for collecting dots while avoiding ghosts, thereby encouraging sustained engagement. The resulting Gaze-Pac-Man prototype was evaluated through a pilot experiment involving healthy participants. Results indicated that the modified version was perceived as more enjoyable than the original, suggesting that such adaptations are a promising avenue for future rehabilitation tools.

We introduce a variational approximation for the brittle fracture energy associated with piecewise-rigid materials. This approach relies on a specific gradient flow formulation to derive an asymptotic expansion of the energy. The leading term in this expansion is quadratic, whereas the remainder term is cubic and remains uniform across the entire domain. We establish this result under the assumption that the material is initially close to a rigid configuration, a condition that can be satisfied by applying a preliminary projection.

We examine the potential for third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks to resolve current anomalies in lepton-flavour non-universality and $B_s$-meson mixing. Our analysis indicates that these leptoquarks can simultaneously account for the $R_{K^{(*)}}$ and $R_{\mu/e}$ anomalies while maintaining consistency with existing bounds from $B_s$ mixing, provided the $b\to s$ couplings are sufficiently suppressed.

Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, while highly effective for detecting and characterizing tumors, poses a significant risk of radiation exposure to patients. This risk is particularly acute for vulnerable groups, such as pregnant women and children, where the potential harm from ionizing radiation may outweigh the diagnostic advantages. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop advanced methods for estimating tumor characteristics using only non-ionizing data. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to predict key tumor features from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. The proposed approach employs a dual-branch architecture: one branch utilizes a ResNet-18 model to extract deep features from MRI images, while the second branch leverages a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to generate synthetic PET images based on those features. These generated images are then used to train a deep neural network for predicting tumor attributes. The method was evaluated on a dataset comprising 1,000 cases of lung cancer patients, demonstrating strong performance with a mean absolute error of 0.19 for tumor volume and 0.19 for standardized uptake value (SUV) maximum.

Although personalization systems are increasingly prevalent, they frequently raise concerns about data gathering and usage. Consequently, this paper introduces a method for collecting data through a natural, personalized experience that remains transparent to users. This approach was evaluated via a study involving 1,000 participants, which demonstrated that the proposed method successfully acquired a substantial amount of data while maintaining high user trust.

Centering theory serves as a robust framework for analyzing the coherence of discourse by examining the relationships between adjacent sentences. This study introduces a novel method for automatically detecting centering shifts within Chinese text, utilizing centering features to segment documents into coherent centering units. Experiments conducted on the Chinese Treebank 2 demonstrate that this approach effectively partitions Chinese corpus into meaningful segments.

An upward planar drawing of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is defined as a planar layout where every directed edge is represented as an upward monotone curve. This paper introduces an $O(n^2)$ algorithm capable of generating such a drawing for any DAG with $n$ vertices, given a specific partial order. This approach improves upon the previously known algorithm by Dujmovi\'c et al., which had a time complexity of $O(n^3)$.

The proliferation of modern, configurable systems underscores the critical need for automation in their configuration processes, thereby enhancing development cycle agility. This paper introduces a novel approach to configuring systems through the use of configuration graphs. These graphs represent configurations as nodes and their interdependencies as edges, enabling the derivation of valid configurations via graph traversal. We present a tool implementing this methodology, which supports incremental development, facilitates the visualization of configurations, and allows for the generation of code from these graphs.

We investigate operator growth and entanglement within quantum systems possessing Lie symmetry. By leveraging the algebraic structure of the underlying symmetry, we derive exact results for the dynamics of out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) and the entanglement entropy of a bipartite setup, where one partition consists of a single symmetric irreducible representation (irrep). Our findings indicate that operator growth is typically non-uniform, often following a power law, and that entanglement entropy exhibits a characteristic "two-level" structure. We further demonstrate that these systems serve as an ideal testing ground for validating numerical algorithms designed to compute OTOCs and entanglement entropy.

WiFi fingerprinting is a prevalent indoor positioning technique that relies on Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) data to determine a user's location. This study introduces a novel approach to enhance positioning accuracy by employing a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network to map signal strength to spatial coordinates. The proposed method was evaluated using a dataset comprising 1,000 reference points collected from the University of Tehran campus. Results indicate that this approach achieves a mean positioning error of 1.8 meters.

A Dyson Sphere is a theoretical megastructure proposed by Freeman Dyson in 1960, designed to encompass a star and capture its energy output. This concept serves as a potential indicator of advanced extraterrestrial civilizations and remains a significant topic in the search for life beyond our solar system. In this paper, we present a novel method for detecting such structures by analyzing the light curves of variable stars located within the central star's vicinity. Our approach relies on identifying specific variations in the light curve of the central star caused by the transit of the megastructure's components. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulations of variable stars situated at different distances from the central star, utilizing both Keplerian and non-Keplerian orbital configurations for the transit bodies.

Networked services have become a primary revenue source for network operators, with Service Level Agreements (SLAs) serving as the mechanism to define service quality and ensure its delivery. Consequently, the ability to accurately forecast SLA traffic is vital for optimizing resource allocation and maximizing revenue. However, the unpredictable nature of SLA traffic patterns poses a significant forecasting challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the concept of "temporal communities" to model SLA traffic. By applying a specific algorithm to identify these communities, the proposed method achieves a 10% improvement in forecasting accuracy compared to existing techniques.

Beam breakup instability (BBI) represents a critical phenomenon in high-energy particle accelerators, imposing strict limits on maximum beam current. This study introduces a novel, rigorous, and comprehensive framework for analyzing BBI within the context of a storage ring. The proposed methodology employs a two-step approach: first, a multi-mode representation of the longitudinal beam distribution is utilized to derive a multi-degree-of-freedom model that captures the essential dynamics of BBI; second, a systematic analysis of the resulting system is conducted to determine the stability of the beam. The validity of this framework is demonstrated through its application to a specific example, where it successfully yields a closed-form expression for the BBI threshold.

Three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers are emerging as a vital technology for neutrino oscillation studies, offering a compact, high-resolution, and cost-effective solution for tracking charged particles. This paper introduces a novel method for reconstructing the three-dimensional trajectories of charged particles within these trackers by integrating a specific light collection geometry with a dedicated reconstruction algorithm. The proposed system utilizes a scintillator layering scheme of 1.0 cm/0.5 cm/0.5 cm (active layer and two readout layers, respectively) combined with a light collection arrangement of 0.5 cm/0.5 cm/0.5 cm (two layers each). The resulting 3D track reconstruction algorithm leverages the distinct light intensity profiles generated by this specific layering configuration. Validation tests were conducted using a 1.0 cm thick scintillator sheet illuminated by a laser line source, demonstrating a spatial resolution of 0.3 mm/0.4 mm in the x/y and z directions, respectively.

This study examines the influence of surface water on the sticking forces between chondritic grains, utilizing molecular dynamics simulations to explore the effects of temperature and water content. Our findings indicate that water significantly enhances adhesion forces, with this increase becoming more pronounced at higher temperatures. Specifically, at 300 K, a water layer 100 monolayers thick results in a sticking force approximately 100 times greater than that of dry grains. We attribute this amplification to the formation of a water bridge between grains, which generates a substantial capillary force. Furthermore, we observed that water facilitates adhesion by reducing the energy barrier for grains to overcome repulsive forces and reach an attractive potential well. These results suggest that water is a critical factor in the early growth of planetesimals.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) serves as a locally linear technique designed to perform dimensionality reduction while preserving class separability. This study introduces LFDA-GL, a novel iterative approach that integrates LFDA with Graph Laplacian Regression. The proposed method constructs both a similarity graph and a class label graph to learn a low-dimensional representation of the data. Theoretical analysis confirms that LFDA-GL is guaranteed to converge. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that LFDA-GL outperforms LFDA and other existing methods in terms of classification accuracy.

Imitation learning enables robots to acquire complex behaviors by observing demonstrations, with extended kernelized movement primitives (EKMP) emerging as a leading approach for representing these skills. Although EKMPs are highly flexible, their computational demands can be prohibitive for real-time applications. This study introduces a novel, computationally efficient approximation of EKMPs that maintains comparable performance. By employing a reduced-dimensional feature space, the proposed method achieves significant reductions in both training and execution times. Furthermore, the approach is designed to be modular, allowing for the integration of various kernel functions. Experimental results confirm that this approximation yields performance nearly indistinguishable from the original EKMPs.

This work examines the central emission vertex (CEV) involving two gluons at one-loop order. The CEV serves as the central element of the BFKL equation, representing the probability amplitude for gluons to emit a gluon cluster at the center of a rapidity gap. We derive a closed-form expression for the CEV by utilizing the known result for the CEV with two fermions, combined with the quark-to-gluon splitting amplitude. Our findings indicate that the one-loop CEV for two gluons is composed of three distinct parts: a component proportional to the square of the CEV for two fermions, a component proportional to the square of the one-loop CEV for two fermions, and a component involving the product of the one-loop CEV for two fermions and the quark-to-gluon splitting amplitude.

We investigate the interplay between Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman field within a two-dimensional $p$-wave superconductor. Our findings indicate that Rashba coupling can stabilize superconductivity under a Zeeman field by shifting the energy of the gapless point away from the Fermi level. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this configuration generates a topological phase characterized by a non-zero Chern number, which hosts gapless Majorana modes at its boundaries.

We present a low-temperature specific heat study of La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ (LSCO) with a Sr doping level of $x=0.07$, conducted under magnetic fields up to 14 T. Our findings indicate that at temperatures below 10 K, the vortex lattice state persists even when the superfluid density is extremely low. Furthermore, we observed that increasing the magnetic field strength enhances the specific heat associated with the vortex lattice, a trend that aligns with theoretical predictions for a vortex liquid state.

This study presents a self-consistent mean-field theory for polymer brushes on curved substrates, explicitly accounting for end exclusion zones. By deriving a new, exact expression for the end density profile, we determine the brush height and the distribution of end exclusion zones across the substrate. Our findings indicate that end exclusion zones are notably more pronounced on concave surfaces compared to convex ones. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these zones significantly influence the scaling behavior of the brush height with respect to the degree of curvature.

In graph theory, the distance between two vertices $u$ and $v$, denoted $d(u,v)$, represents the length of the shortest path connecting them. A set $W$ is termed a resolving set if the distance vector from any vertex $v$ to each element in $W$ uniquely identifies $v$. The minimum cardinality of such a set defines the graph's metric dimension. This study introduces the concept of a $k$-resolving set, where the distance vector from any vertex $v$ to $k$ vertices in the set uniquely determines $v$. The minimum size of a $k$-resolving set is referred to as the $k$-dimension. We derive the $k$-dimension for specific graph families, including paths, cycles, wheels, and complete graphs. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the $k$-dimension of any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, given by $\lceil \log_{k+1} n \rceil + k$. Finally, we demonstrate that the $k$-dimension of the Cartesian product of two graphs $G$ and $H$ is bounded above by the sum of their individual $k$-dimensions, i.e., $dim_k(G \square H) \le dim_k(G) + dim_k(H)$.

Space telescopes capture astronomical images by stacking multiple exposures, a process that is time-intensive and prone to errors. This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to enhance the stacking of images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWB), specifically addressing the challenges of aligning and integrating data from the Near-Infrared Imager and Slitless Spectrograph (NIRISS). We developed a deep learning model that utilizes a U-Net architecture to simultaneously perform image alignment and integration. Our approach trains on simulated NIRISS image sets, employing a loss function that prioritizes the preservation of faint astronomical sources. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves alignment accuracy within 0.5 pixels and successfully recovers faint sources with a 10% improvement in signal-to-noise ratio compared to traditional stacking methods.

This paper investigates the performance of serial dictatorship mechanisms for combinatorial optimization problems. We introduce a general algorithmic framework that enables the derivation of constant-factor approximation guarantees for a wide range of social welfare objectives. Specifically, we demonstrate that this approach yields a 2-approximation for the egalitarian welfare measure and a 3-approximation for the Nash welfare measure.

We have discovered a new binary asteroid, designated 2000 QG10, which features a primary body with a diameter of 1.9 kilometers and a secondary body of 0.45 kilometers, separated by a distance of 3.0 kilometers. This discovery is significant because it represents the widest known binary pair among asteroids larger than 1 kilometer in diameter. The system's orbital period is 13.5 hours, and its configuration is dynamically stable, with the secondary body orbiting at approximately 2.5 Hill radii. Furthermore, the analysis of lightcurve data and the system's geometry allowed us to determine the mass of the primary asteroid, which is $1.1 \times 10^{12}$ kilograms. The discovery of such widely separated binaries provides crucial insights into the mechanisms of binary formation and the physical properties of large asteroids.

This paper provides a concise overview of the large-sample properties of estimators and test statistics commonly applied in econometric modeling. It examines the asymptotic distributions of these tools across various model specifications, including linear regression, autoregressive frameworks, time-varying parameter systems, and vector autoregressions. Furthermore, the text outlines the asymptotic behavior of likelihood ratio tests, Wald tests, and score tests within both linear and nonlinear least squares contexts.

This study introduces a generalized Riemann-Liouville fractional integral defined by a function $\omega$ and establishes several fundamental properties, including the commutativity of the generalized Riemann-Liouville fractional integral and derivative, as well as product, quotient, and chain rules applicable to these operators. Additionally, the paper derives new fractional inequalities, specifically the Chebyshev- type inequality and the Grüss inequality, within the framework of generalized Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals.

This study investigates the application of a regularized least-squares (LS) approach for demodulation in large-scale multiuser spatial modulation (SM) MIMO systems. In these setups, each transmitter employs multiple antennas, but only one is active per symbol interval. The proposed regularized LS method is evaluated against the conventional LS technique and maximum likelihood (ML) detection. Simulation outcomes indicate that the regularized LS method achieves performance comparable to ML detection while offering a substantial reduction in computational complexity.

Spectral energy distributions (SEDs) serve as a fundamental tool for analyzing galaxies, yet their application is frequently hindered by the lack of a standardized definition and consistent methodology. This study introduces a formal definition of an SED and outlines a reproducible approach to generate them using multi-wavelength photometric data. We demonstrate that these generated SEDs are highly effective for comparing galaxies and analyzing their evolutionary histories. Furthermore, we show that these methods can be applied to both individual objects and entire galaxy populations.

The South Atlantic rift basin originated from the breakup of the South American and African continents, a process that commenced approximately 130 million years ago. This study utilizes a new, high-resolution, full waveform seismic tomographic model of the upper mantle beneath the South Atlantic to investigate the deep-seated mantle dynamics responsible for this rifting event. Our model reveals a distinct, narrow vertical structure extending from the surface down to depths of 600 km, situated directly beneath the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP). This feature is flanked by two broader, low-velocity anomalies on either side. We propose that this narrow structure represents a deep mantle conduit that facilitated the upwelling of hot material, thereby driving the rifting process. Furthermore, the model indicates that the lateral boundaries of this conduit are defined by the subduction of ancient oceanic lithosphere, which occurred prior to the initial continental separation.

Unsupervised pre-training has emerged as a powerful strategy for enhancing model performance in downstream tasks, particularly when labeled data is scarce. This paper introduces a novel approach to unsupervised pre-training for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that leverages the inherent structural properties of graphs. Specifically, we introduce the Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) framework, which employs a graph-level contrastive objective to create discriminative graph representations. GCL operates by generating two augmented versions of each graph through stochastic node masking and applies a contrastive loss to maximize the similarity between these views. We further demonstrate that GCL can be extended to generate node-level embeddings by incorporating a reconstruction loss alongside the contrastive objective. Extensive experiments across multiple graph classification and node classification benchmarks illustrate that GCL yields state-of-the-art results, surpassing existing methods in both pre-training quality and downstream task performance.

We introduce a formal framework for role-playing games like Dungeons and Dragons, utilizing it to analyze the impact of the Dungeon Master's decisions on player outcomes. In this model, the Dungeon Master selects a scenario and the subsequent sequence of events, with the player's choices constrained by the specific scenario and the ruleset. We demonstrate that the Dungeon Master can strategically manipulate the game's difficulty to maximize revenue by optimizing difficulty levels to balance player engagement with profitability.

This study introduces a new framework for automatically detecting lexical semantic shifts, termed "change discovery," which encompasses both traditional "change detection" and the identification of novel senses. While change detection focuses on pinpointing the specific timeframe when an existing sense emerges or vanishes, change discovery aims to locate instances of a sense within texts, regardless of whether that sense is established or emerging. To achieve this, we developed a method that integrates a sense definition model with a change discovery algorithm. The model employs a multi-task learning approach, utilizing a bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) based language model alongside a sense definition classifier. This classifier is trained to predict both the sense of a target word and the specific type of semantic change occurring. The proposed change discovery algorithm leverages these predictions to identify instances of sense usage. We evaluated this framework on two datasets: one designed for change detection and another for change discovery. Results indicate that the method successfully identifies instances of both new and existing senses, with a particular emphasis on capturing instances of emerging senses.

We introduce a novel set of $k$-dependent functions, $T_1^{\perp g}(x, k_\perp)$, which are defined through the correlation of a quark's spin vector with the transverse component of the total hadron's angular momentum. These functions emerge as the transverse-angular-momentum counterparts to the standard transverse-momentum-dependent (T-PDF) $T_1^{\perp}(x, k_\perp)$, which relies on a quark's longitudinal spin. We derive the corresponding evolution equations for these new distributions and establish their connection to the $k$-dependent functions associated with the transverse spin of a gluon.

This study introduces a new method for characterizing knotoids by integrating topological and geometric features. We define the "knotoid signature" as a composite vector comprising the self-intersection number, the writhe, the linking number, and the normalized distance between the free ends. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we analyze a dataset of 1,000 knotoids derived from the Knotoid Atlas. Our findings reveal that knotoid signatures effectively organize these structures into distinct clusters, thereby offering a robust framework for the classification of knotoids.

Early dark energy (EDE) is proposed as a solution to the Hubble Tension, yet its impact on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) remains limited to a narrow epoch. This study introduces a novel EDE model based on a scalar field coupled to curvature, which is capable of generating a significant energy density during the early universe while naturally decaying to negligible levels later on. We demonstrate that this model can effectively alleviate the Hubble Tension with parameter values closely resembling those of the standard EDE framework. Furthermore, we show that this model remains consistent with current observations of large-scale structure and the cosmic shear signal.

This work demonstrates that the group of symplectic mapping classes for the one-point symplectic blowup of a manifold $X$, specifically regarding the $\mathbb{Z}_k$-blowup of the 4-torus's Kähler form on the 4-torus, is generated by Dehn twists along certain 2-spheres.

This study examines the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem within the framework of an $O(N)$-symmetric $\sigma$-model, where a local $U(1)$ subgroup remains unbroken. We derive a violation of the standard NG counting rule, demonstrating that the number of NG modes is $N-2$ rather than the expected $N-1$. Furthermore, we establish that the NG modes associated with the broken generators are not independent, as their commutator yields a non-vanishing central charge. This central charge modifies the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, thereby preventing the simultaneous precise measurement of the corresponding NG fields.

We introduce DISCO, a novel framework designed to create high-quality, diverse, and semantically meaningful counterfactual data for machine learning models. Unlike existing methods that rely on heuristic rules or specific model architectures, DISCO leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate counterfactuals by optimizing a loss function that balances adherence to factual constraints with semantic diversity. We further enhance this process using a reinforcement learning approach to refine the optimization. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that DISCO outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in generating diverse, varied, and high-quality counterfactuals.

This paper investigates the total chromatic number of circulant graphs, denoted as $\chi_t(Cay(\mathbb{Z}_n,S))$, where $n$ is an even integer and $S$ is a symmetric generating set. We establish that $\chi_t(\text{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_n,S)) = \Delta+1$, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum degree, under the condition that $4$ divides $n$ and $n/2 \notin S$. Additionally, we demonstrate that $\chi_t(\text{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_n,S)) = \Delta+2$ when $n/2 \in S$.

Remote epitaxy, a phenomenon where a substrate's crystal lattice influences a distant overlayer, is typically observed only within a few atomic layers. This study demonstrates that the influence of a substrate can extend significantly further, as evidenced by the growth of a Heusler compound, CoMn$_2$Sb, on graphene supported by GaAs. The presence of remote epitaxy is supported by the discovery of a novel Moiré superlattice in the overlying CoMn$_2$Sb layer, which exhibits a periodicity of 1.5 nm. This specific period corresponds to a superlattice formed by the interference of two distinct contributions: a 1.5 nm Moiré pattern resulting from the interaction between the GaAs substrate and the overlayer, and a 1.0 nm Moiré pattern arising from the interference of the overlayer's own domains. These findings indicate that remote epitaxy can persist over distances of at least 10 nm.

This study examines the concept of linear $L$-invariant subspaces within the group $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive code framework, where an additive code $C$ is defined as a subspace of $\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$. We introduce a novel class of $L$-linear codes, termed $L$-linear codes, and establish a one-to-one correspondence between these $L$-invariant subspaces and the newly defined $L$-linear codes. Furthermore, we derive the Gray mapping for $L$-invariant subspaces and determine their minimum distance.

This study introduces a novel graded viscosity bank technology, designed to enhance the efficiency of polymer flooding by integrating a leading-edge polymer injection strategy with a well arrangement that creates a graded viscosity bank. The proposed approach involves injecting a primary polymer solution to establish a leading polymer bank, followed by the injection of a secondary solution to form a trailing bank. This dual-stage process generates a distinct viscosity gradient within the leading bank, thereby optimizing sweep efficiency. Numerical simulations utilizing the CMG-GEM model were conducted to evaluate the performance of this graded viscosity bank against standard leading bank methods. Results indicate that the proposed technique increases oil recovery by 11.3% relative to the conventional leading bank approach. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the performance benefits of this graded system are highly sensitive to the specific placement of the leading bank.

Conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) have become a dominant approach for class-conditional generation, enabling the creation of diverse data samples by incorporating auxiliary information into the training process. However, the effectiveness of these models is highly sensitive to the quality of that auxiliary input. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to automatically refine the auxiliary training data through an end-to-end refinement loop. In this architecture, a refinement network generates improved versions of the input, while a dedicated critic evaluates the resulting generator outputs. We demonstrate the method's efficacy on two distinct tasks: generating synthetic images from noisy inputs and creating 3D point clouds from 2D images.

This study introduces a novel, robust numerical scheme designed to address the time-fractional phase-field Cahn-Hilliard equation, utilizing a modified energy framework. The approach discretizes the equation in both time and space, employing a second-order finite difference method for spatial dimensions and a first-order energy-dissipating technique for time. The method's stability is established through the application of a specific energy definition, while convergence is demonstrated via a rigorous error analysis. Numerical simulations are provided to validate both the theoretical findings and the scheme's practical performance.

We examine the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) construction, which maps a C*-algebra and a state to a Hilbert space, as a functor. We demonstrate that this functor is fully faithful and possesses a left adjoint.

We present a new method for estimating the accretion rate of active galactic nuclei (AGN) by utilizing the spectral energy distribution (SED) of their radio and optical/UV emissions. This approach relies on the assumption that AGN possess a common spectral shape across the radio-to-UV range, which is governed by the magnetic field strength and the age of the electron population. We demonstrate that this technique is particularly effective for radio galaxies (RGs) with masses exceeding $10^{10} M_{\odot}$ and luminosity distances greater than 100 Mpc. By applying this method to the Fermi-LAT catalog of GeV sources, we identified a subset of radio galaxies that emit GeV radiation at accretion rates of $\dot{M} \gtrsim 10^{-2} M_{\odot} \text{yr}^{-1}$. These findings suggest that GeV emission in massive radio galaxies originates from the central regions of their accretion disks, where the radiative efficiency is high.

This study introduces a novel methodology for estimating the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of portfolio returns by leveraging the empirical CDF of their corresponding efficient frontier. We demonstrate that the efficient frontier of a portfolio's feasible region, defined by its variance and expected return, serves as a nonparametric representation of the portfolio's return distribution. Consequently, we propose a novel estimator for the CDF of portfolio returns by utilizing the efficient frontier as a basis. We further establish the strong consistency of this proposed estimator. Finally, we apply this method to analyze the distribution of returns for various U.S. equity portfolios.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a fundamental, non-invasive method for detecting heart diseases, relying on the analysis of heart sounds. However, this process is heavily dependent on the expertise of medical practitioners, which can lead to inconsistencies. To address this limitation, this study introduces a deep learning framework designed to automate heart sound classification. The proposed system employs a hybrid architecture that integrates a ResNet-50 backbone with a multi-scale attention mechanism. This approach enables the model to extract robust features from heart sounds while effectively capturing multi-scale contextual information. The framework was evaluated using a dataset comprising 1,000 heart sound recordings from 10 distinct classes. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.99 and an accuracy of 0.98, demonstrating its high performance and reliability.

Wearable health technology has become increasingly popular, yet it remains underutilized for data aggregation and personalization due to two primary obstacles: the difficulty of extracting information from diverse devices and the challenge of creating user-specific applications. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework that leverages the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the extraction of data from various wearable platforms. Furthermore, this framework utilizes LLMs to generate personalized applications by synthesizing extracted data with existing knowledge. We evaluated our approach using a dataset comprising 1,000 samples from 100 users across 10 different wearable devices. Results indicate that our method achieves an average F1 score of 0.85 for data extraction and successfully produces personalized applications for 99% of the users.

This study introduces a novel portfolio optimization strategy that incorporates skewness and kurtosis as higher moments. By utilizing a Taylor series expansion, the model derives the dynamics of these moments, which are subsequently integrated into a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). These ODEs are solved to generate the optimal portfolio weights. The proposed approach is validated through both numerical simulations and empirical data analysis.

We examine the potential for dark energy to emerge from string theory compactifications on Calabi-Yau threefolds, specifically within the context of $\alpha'$ corrections. Our analysis indicates that, in the absence of non-geometric fluxes, the resulting cosmological constant is invariably negative. Conversely, incorporating these fluxes allows for a positive value of $\Lambda$; however, this comes at the cost of a large positive scalar curvature, which is incompatible with the flat geometry required for our macroscopic spacetime.

Recruiting new employees is a critical function for any organization, yet the interview scheduling process often involves complex challenges. In large corporations, numerous candidates must be interviewed by multiple interviewers, with the need to coordinate various constraints to create an efficient plan. This study introduces a novel approach to interview scheduling that leverages a multi-agent system. Within this framework, each agent represents a specific role, such as a candidate, an interviewer, or a scheduling manager, and they collaborate to generate an optimal plan. The proposed method utilizes a hierarchical multi-agent architecture, where agents operate at different levels of abstraction to manage the process. Additionally, the paper outlines a specific scheduling protocol designed to facilitate coordination among these agents. Experimental results demonstrate that this method successfully produces effective interview schedules.

This study examines switching control problems characterized by discontinuous costs at regime transitions. We establish the existence of an optimal cost function that is continuous and satisfies a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation with specific transmission conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a vanishing viscosity approximation converges to this optimal cost function.

We introduce a novel type of leptoquark pair production, termed asymmetric leptoquark pair production, which occurs when a lepton collides with a leptoquark. This process is distinct from standard leptoquark pair creation, which requires lepton-proton collisions. We examine the potential of the International Linear Collider (ILC) to detect this phenomenon, specifically analyzing scenarios where the leptoquark is a scalar carrying $B-L$ quantum numbers. Our findings indicate that the ILC can achieve a $5\sigma$ discovery sensitivity for leptoquark masses up to $1.5$ TeV, provided the production cross-section exceeds $0.05$ pb.

Temporal sequences are ubiquitous in various domains, ranging from neuroscience to finance. While numerous methods exist for analyzing these time series, they often struggle to effectively capture the underlying dynamics of complex systems. To address this limitation, we introduce Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), a novel approach that integrates supervised learning with dynamic topological mapping. This method enables the simultaneous reconstruction of both the input data space and the target output space, while explicitly modeling the temporal evolution connecting them. SGTM-TT achieves this by combining a supervised learning component with a topological mapping technique. Specifically, it utilizes a neural network to learn a mapping between the input and output spaces, with its parameters optimized via supervised learning. Furthermore, the method employs a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a low-dimensional latent representation of the input data, which evolves over time to generate the corresponding outputs. We demonstrate the efficacy of SGTM-TT through an application to calcium imaging data, where it successfully recovers the latent dynamics of neural activity and accurately predicts associated behavioral outputs.

We present a detailed analysis of the 2.3 $\mu$m C I and C II lines in the nearby galaxy M 33, utilizing the GEMINI/GMCA spectral decomposition to derive their spatial distribution and kinematics. Our findings reveal that the C I and C II lines are spatially and kinematically distinct, with the C I emission being significantly broader and more extended than that of C II. Furthermore, the C I line exhibits a complex morphology that cannot be adequately modeled by a single component, necessitating a two-component fit to accurately represent the data. We attribute the broadening of the C I line to non-LTE excitation, which arises from the spatial decoupling between the C I and C II emissions. This non-LTE effect results in an overestimation of the molecular gas velocity dispersion by a factor of approximately 1.5. Consequently, this overestimation leads to an underestimation of molecular gas temperatures by roughly 100 K. These findings have significant implications for interpreting molecular gas properties in other galaxies, particularly those with low metallicity.

We present a new, model-independent approach to determining the CKM angle $\gamma$ by utilizing the CP violation observed in Kaon decay. This method relies on the interference between $b \to c\bar{c}s$ and $b \to u\bar{u}s$ transitions within the $B^0_s$–$\bar{B}^0_s$ mixing system. The technique is applicable to the decay $B^0_s \to K^+ \pi^- \pi^0$, where the final state is reconstructed via the intermediate resonance $K_S^0 \pi^0$.

The sequence reconstruction problem involves a source sending a sequence through $n$ channels, where each channel independently recovers the sequence with a probability $p$. The objective is to determine the minimum $k$ channels necessary for the source to reconstruct the transmitted sequence with a probability exceeding $1/2$. This study examines the scenario where the alphabet size is $q=3$ and the Hamming distance threshold is $d=1$. We demonstrate that the minimum $k$ is approximately $1.585n$ and provide a proof for the lower bound of $1.5849n$.

Hierarchical approaches are frequently employed to enhance few-shot learning performance in musical instrument classification. This study introduces a novel hierarchical framework that incorporates a coarse-grained level for broad instrument families alongside a fine-grained level for specific instrument types. By utilizing a coarse-grained classifier to filter out irrelevant instruments, the proposed method reduces the number of distracting options presented to the model during the classification task. Experiments conducted on the Music21 dataset demonstrate that this hierarchical strategy yields superior results compared to standard hierarchical few-shot learning methods.

Current Question Answering systems often fail to effectively interpret academic papers, a limitation that hinders their utility in the research community. To address this, we introduce QASPER, an end-to-end QA framework designed for scientific literature. Our method utilizes a multi-stage approach that integrates various components, including a specialized module for extracting named entities and a technique for generating answers through the combination of multiple named entity mentions. We evaluated our system on the SQuaLiP dataset, which consists of over 10,000 questions targeting named entity mentions within the arXiv corpus. Our results demonstrate that our method achieves a 60.0% F1 score on the test set, outperforming both prior end-to-end models and strong baselines.

Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) are sensitive to gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) via their Hulse-Taylor radiation, which is characterized by a single frequency and amplitude. This paper evaluates three methods for calculating these signals: the standard approach, a simplified approximation, and a new, even more efficient technique. The results indicate that the simplified method offers the fastest evaluation speed while maintaining a discrepancy of less than 1% compared to the exact signal.

This study examines the large-time asymptotic behavior of the two-point correlation function for a second-class particle within the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP), specifically in the bulk of the lattice away from boundaries. By leveraging the integrability of the model, we derive a rigorous derivation of the asymptotic formula previously conjectured by Corwin, O'Connell, Corwyn, and Seppäläinen. Our approach involves analyzing the double contour integral representation of the correlation function, where the integrand is expressed as a double sum of determinants. We demonstrate that, in the limit of large time, the dominant contribution to the integral arises from a specific set of poles, thereby establishing the validity of the conjectured result.

This study examines the Kermack-McKendrick epidemic models, covering both age-of-infection formulations and their age-stratified variants. It analyzes the problem of identifying a generation time distribution from observed epidemic curves, addressing scenarios where the distribution is either arbitrary or restricted to specific parametric families. The work establishes the existence of solutions, investigates their uniqueness, and provides numerical methods for implementation.

Majorana fermions represent exotic particles that lack a distinct antiparticle counterpart, emerging as a phenomenon in condensed matter systems. This study introduces a Majorana fermionic formulation of the two-dimensional Hubbard model, utilizing a fermionic coherent state approach to construct a corresponding path integral. We demonstrate that this Majorana representation yields results identical to those obtained from a standard fermionic representation. Furthermore, we derive a Majorana-based slave-rotor representation for the model. By applying this framework to examine the doped $t$-$J$ model, we derive a Majorana fermionic slave-rotor form of the $t$-$P$ model. Finally, we show that the Majorana slave-rotor formulation of the $t$-$P$ model is equivalent to the well-established Majorana $t$-$J$ model proposed by Matsumoto and Takahashi.

Acronyms are prevalent in written language, yet their frequent use can hinder readability and understanding, particularly for readers unfamiliar with the specific abbreviations. This study introduces a novel method for automatically generating acronyms by leveraging the contextual information surrounding their initial occurrences. The proposed approach employs a bidirectional encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder processes the local textual context and the decoder constructs the corresponding acronym. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both generating acronyms and correctly identifying them.

We present a theoretical framework for generating atom-molecule pairs, comprising one molecule and one free atom, starting from a Bose-Einstein condensate of spin-zero atoms. Our analysis demonstrates that, contrary to the conventional view, these pairs can be produced via a two-step mechanism initiated by spin-exchange collisions that generate spin-1 atoms, followed by photoassociation targeting those spin-1 components to form molecules in the $|1,1\rangle$ state, which subsequently collide with remaining spin-zero atoms. This approach is applicable to $^{87}\text{Rb}$ and other alkali species.

We introduce a new DNA-storage architecture that leverages the parallelism of DNA synthesis and sequencing to create a system where data is organized into pools, with each pool containing numerous documents. This approach contrasts with previous methods that synthesized and sequenced data individually, thereby enabling more efficient storage and retrieval. To facilitate data access, we propose a novel index structure that maps documents to their respective pools. Furthermore, we present a new encoding scheme that facilitates rapid data updates. Our experimental results indicate that this architecture achieves a 100-fold reduction in sequencing costs for data retrieval and a 1000-fold reduction in sequencing costs for updates when compared to existing technologies.

Topological insulators are characterized by conducting surface states protected by time-reversal symmetry, which exhibit spin-momentum locking and are immune to backscattering from non-magnetic impurities. This study investigates the transport properties of a topological insulator in the presence of an external magnetic field, specifically examining the interplay between its surface and bulk states. We demonstrate that the surface states of a topological insulator can be decoupled from its bulk states through the application of a magnetic field. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism allows for the generation of a pure Quantum Hall effect arising solely from the surface states, a phenomenon that is distinct from the conventional Quantum Hall effect observed in bulk materials.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the primary modality for detecting and diagnosing brain tumors. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to segment brain tumors using MRI data. The proposed approach integrates a three-dimensional U-Net architecture with a residual connection to enhance segmentation performance. Additionally, a novel loss function combining Dice coefficient and cross-entropy is employed to address class imbalance and improve model robustness. Evaluated on the BraTS 2019 dataset, the method achieved a Dice score of 0.799, an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.699, and a sensitivity of 0.899. These outcomes indicate that the suggested technique offers a highly effective solution for brain tumor segmentation.

Differentiable rendering serves as a powerful tool for addressing image-based inverse problems by integrating physical scene models with optimization techniques. This paper introduces a differentiable differentiator designed to handle various rendering architectures, enabling the optimization of parameters within each specific model. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through several applications, including the optimization of neural radiance fields, implicit surfaces, and deep convolutional networks.

Interlacing remains a prevalent method for displaying moving images, offering a cost-effective solution that delivers high resolution and refresh rates by splitting each frame into two sequential fields. This study introduces a novel, hardware-efficient architecture designed to implement an interlaced-to-progressive converter specifically for 1080i/1080p video signals. The proposed design operates at a 1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/1080p/

This study examines the root mean square radius of the point neutron distribution ($R_{p,n}$) within the relativistic mean-field (RMF) and relativistic random-phase approximation (RPA) frameworks. Our findings indicate that the RPA correction to $R_{p,n}$ is contingent upon the neutron skin thickness and the nuclear incompressibility. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the RPA contribution to $R_{p,n}$ is governed by the strength of the isoscalar monopole residual interaction, which is directly linked to the magnitude of the effective nucleon interaction in the isoscalar channel.

This study introduces a novel application of machine learning (ML) to predict river flow velocities, utilizing data derived from a high-fidelity numerical solver. The research focuses on the Navier-Stokes equations, employing a deep neural network (DNN) trained on a dataset of flow configurations. The DNN is designed to learn a mapping between these configurations and their corresponding velocity fields, enabling rapid predictions for new scenarios. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through a specific case study involving a river with a complex, irregular geometry. Results indicate that the proposed ML approach achieves high accuracy, with a maximum error of approximately 0.001 m/s, while offering a computational speedup of roughly 100,000 times compared to traditional solvers.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging multiple exposures of the same scene to capture a wider dynamic range than a single shot allows. This study introduces a new technique for generating such images using a single exposure, relying on a learned tone-mapping operator. This approach involves merging a set of tone-mapped images derived from the original capture through varying levels of exposure compensation. The resulting merged image serves as the final HDR output. The proposed tone-mapping operator is formulated as a sparse linear combination of basis functions, where the coefficients are determined via a learned dictionary. The proposed sparse representation framework is solved using an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

Causal deep learning is emerging as a promising avenue for enhancing both predictive accuracy and reasoning capabilities within machine learning. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent advancements in this field, with a specific focus on methodologies that integrate causality into neural architectures. We examine key approaches, including the incorporation of causal reasoning, the utilization of causal representations, and the application of causal structures to deepen models. Furthermore, we outline several promising future research trajectories in causal deep learning.

This study presents a numerical investigation into the temperature profiles of a catalytic fixed bed reactor, utilizing a one-dimensional two-phase model. The model incorporates the Ergun equation to describe pressure drop and applies the axial dispersion framework to represent mass and heat transfer. The primary objective is to analyze how variations in inlet temperature and flow rate influence the thermal distribution within the bed. The findings indicate that the model is highly sensitive to these operating parameters, with the flow rate exerting a more pronounced effect on temperature profiles than inlet temperature. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the proposed model accurately captures the physical phenomena observed in the system.

This paper extends the concept of a $\mathfrak{p}$-principle, originally defined by the second author for oriented colored submersions, to the case of oriented colored broken submersions. As an application, we derive a formula for this extended $\mathfrak{p}$-principle specifically regarding these structures.

This study evaluates the performance of the Block Diagonal (BD) and Schur Complement (SC) preconditioners within a multigrid framework for cardiac mechanics simulations. The research focuses on the robustness of these preconditioners across varying mesh resolutions and material parameters. Numerical outcomes indicate that the BD preconditioner is more efficient than the SC approach, particularly regarding the solution of the Dirichlet boundary conditions.

We introduce a specific class of non-crossing pair-partitions defined by a fixed set of integers, demonstrating that the generating function for these partitions yields a moment generating function for a family of moments characterized by a fixed parameter. By applying this result alongside the method of free convolution, we derive an explicit formula for the $\lambda$-deformed semi-circular distribution.

AI-empowered persuasive video generation aims to create videos that influence viewers' decisions or actions through a three-stage workflow: content planning, content production, and content refinement. This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in each phase, with a specific emphasis on AI-driven strategies for generating persuasive videos. We categorize these approaches based on the underlying techniques used in the planning and refinement stages. Furthermore, we outline the current challenges and potential future trajectories for this emerging field.

Gradient masking has long been suspected to act as an effective adversarial defense, yet it remains difficult to verify definitively. This paper introduces a novel, practical method for detecting such masking by leveraging the relationship between the true gradient and its empirical counterpart. Our approach involves training a surrogate model to mimic the gradient outputs of the target model; if the target exhibits masking, the surrogate will fail to learn effectively. We demonstrate that this technique successfully identifies gradient masking in various scenarios where traditional methods have failed.

This study introduces bianisotropic acoustic metagratings designed to manipulate the scattering of surface acoustic waves (SAWs). By integrating a SAW transducer with a periodic array of metallic posts, we achieve full control over SAW phase and amplitude, enabling the manipulation of both the diffraction orders and the acoustic wavefront. Numerical simulations and experimental results confirm that these metagratings can selectively activate specific diffraction orders and shape acoustic wavefronts. These capabilities offer significant potential for applications in ultrasound imaging, nondestructive evaluation, and acoustic beamforming.

Standard diffusion is characterized by a Gaussian distribution of displacements over time, whereas anomalous diffusion follows a power-law scaling. While the continuous time random walk (CTRW) model has historically been used to explain anomalous diffusion, it relies on the assumption of uncorrelated jumps, which fails to capture the long-range correlations observed in many real-world systems. This study introduces a novel model of anomalous diffusion that incorporates long-range correlated jumps, demonstrating that it yields a power-law distribution of displacements consistent with experimental data from human movement, animal foraging, and financial markets. Furthermore, the model is shown to be mathematically equivalent to fractional Brownian motion.

Linear coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity can jointly generate a wide variety of intriguing optical phenomena, including solitons, bound states in the continuum, and exceptional points. This study introduces a general theoretical framework for analyzing such systems, utilizing a two-mode model to examine the interplay between coupling and nonlinearity. We demonstrate that this interaction yields diverse dynamical behaviors, ranging from bistability and multistability to oscillatory responses and complex chaos. Furthermore, we show that by adjusting the coupling strength, one can induce a transition from multistability to chaos, thereby generating a chaotic attractor characterized by a positive Lyapunov exponent and a corresponding bifurcation diagram.

This study examines the global asymptotic controllability and sample stabilizability of stochastic control systems with control-dependent noise. We demonstrate that the existence of a control Lyapunov function is both necessary and sufficient for these properties, and we establish the equivalence between a control Lyapunov function and a control barrier function. Furthermore, we present a constructive method for generating control barrier functions based on a known control Lyapunov function.

We introduce a deep learning framework designed to reconstruct high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from low-resolution measurements. This approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on direct numerical simulation (DNS) data of turbulent channel flow. The model learns to map low-resolution velocity fields to their high-resolution counterparts, effectively capturing the missing turbulent fluctuations. Our method achieves a 100-fold reduction in computational cost compared to traditional direct numerical simulation while maintaining accuracy comparable to DNS. Furthermore, the network generalizes well to data from simulations with varying Reynolds numbers, indicating its robustness across different flow regimes.

This work presents a derivation of the electromagnetic potentials and fields for a point charge moving along an arbitrary trajectory, demonstrating that these results satisfy the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations under the Lorenz gauge condition. We establish that the resulting four-potential adheres to the continuity equation, thereby ensuring the consistency of charge and current conservation. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding Lagrangian for a point charge interacting with an electromagnetic field, proving its equivalence to the standard Lagrangian found in classical electrodynamics.

Confidence calibration is essential for ensuring that machine learning systems function reliably and safely. While various methods exist to improve calibration, they often fail to account for the fact that different input samples possess varying levels of difficulty. This study introduces a novel approach that simultaneously addresses both difficulty-aware calibration and uncertainty quantification. Our method employs a hierarchical Bayesian framework to model difficulty as a latent variable, utilizing a Gaussian Process to represent the difficulty distribution. Furthermore, we propose a new hierarchical Dirichlet process mixture model to capture the complex structure of difficulty among inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both calibration accuracy and uncertainty estimation.

Although reinforcement learning has achieved notable success in various domains, its applications to open-world scenarios remain limited. A primary obstacle is the tendency of RL models to converge to suboptimal local policies, a problem that is particularly acute in complex, dynamic environments. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the diversity of expert knowledge found in large language models (LLMs). Our method utilizes a specialized reward function to guide a policy toward selecting the most suitable LLM for specific tasks, thereby capitalizing on their varied strengths. We evaluated this framework on the OpenAssistant project, a real-world open-source RL system designed to train chat assistants. Results indicate that our approach yields a substantial performance boost compared to standard RL baselines.

Process discovery methods aim to generate process models from event logs. Although numerous approaches exist, they often yield models that are either overly complex or fail to align with actual system behavior. This study introduces a new technique for discovering process models by integrating a specific workflow pattern into the input log. The proposed method utilizes a modified version of the Alpha algorithm to extract sub-logs corresponding to instances of the embedded pattern, then reconstructs the full model by merging these sub-logs. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through an illustrative example.

Light localization in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals is followed by a transition to a delocalized state upon increasing quasiperiodic modulation strength, a phenomenon we identify as light anti-localization. We demonstrate that this anti-localization arises from the coexistence of two distinct types of localized light modes.
